newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks to limit NATO expansion, placate allies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks to limit NATO expansion, placate allies.

text.p: President Bill Clinton goes to Europe this week, determined both to limit the first wave of NATO's expansion to three nations and to assuage the concerns of those countries left out.

U.S. officials and analysts say they expect the July 8-9 Madrid summit that will invite nations to begin negotiations for membership in the Western security alliance to embrace only the U.S. choices: Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

"What I expect to happen in Madrid is that where there is consensus -- that is around the three -- there will be an invitation to begin accession talks," U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told reporters last week.

Eastward expansion has proved one of the more contentious matters for the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) in the post-Cold War era, pitting the United States against some of its allies, notably France and Italy.
While the U.S. wants to keep NATO's initial expansion to three, France has argued strenuously in favour of Romania and Italy on behalf of Slovenia.
But few analysts expect any of the countries now in NATO, whose decisions are made by consensus, to risk splitting the 16-member alliance and derailing enlargment by vetoing the U.S. position.

"In the end the political leaders in all these countries are going to have to decide whether they need to show some flexibility in order to keep the alliance healthy, and my guess is ... they will," said Brookings Institution foreign policy analyst Helmut Sonnenfelt.
Even Romania itself appears to have given up any hope of catching the first wave, with President Emil Constantinescu telling reporters on Friday the matter was a "closed chapter."

On the U.S. side, there appears to be a concerted effort to assuage the concerns of those who will be left out, both by insisting NATO's door will remain open and by a coordinated series of trips to the region from the president on down.

To congratulate the winners and sweeten the pill for the losers, Clinton is scheduled to travel to Poland and Romania after Madrid; Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to the Czech Republic and Slovenia; and Defence Secretary William Cohen to Hungary and Bulgaria.
Speaking to reporters last week, Berger presented the outlines of another effort to allay the concerns of former Warsaw Pact members who do not make the first round.

The national security adviser said he hoped Madrid would endorse a "robust" open-door policy for NATO and the creation of a Euro-Atlantic council, which would serve as a political analogue to the Partnership for Peace programme.

Sonnenfelt of the Brookings Institution argued that the United States must also make more of an effort to placate its allies, many of whom were dismayed by the firm U.S. stance to keep the first round of NATO expansion to three.

"There is going to have to be a less peremptory style," he said. "The Europeans were upset about the public announcement about the U.S. position on the three and there has to be some attention paid to the Europeans' sensitivity on this point."
U.S. officials seem to have little doubt their position will prevail and are untroubled by the possibility that they may be seen as heavy-handed.

"We acknowledge that sometimes the United States has to speak bluntly and candidly but I think they would acknowledge, even if it's privately, that in some way that's the way things get done in this alliance," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters on Friday.
Asked if he expected the matter to be settled by the start of the Madrid summit, Berger made no promises, but then said with a laugh: "It will be resolved before we leave Madrid."
